title: The only gift
hookLine: the only true gift is a portion of yourself (Gifts, 1844)

cards: It's late, the birthday is tomorrow, and the shopping site promises it can still arrive in time. A candle. A nice mug.
A gift card in a bright envelope. Click, done. Nothing wrong with any of it, and plenty of people are glad to get a gift card.
But in a short essay called Gifts, Emerson sets a higher bar, with one blunt sentence about jewelry that can stop a reader short.

teach.b: First, the blunt sentence: "Rings and other jewels are not gifts, but apologies for gifts. The only gift is a portion of thyself."
An apology for a gift: as if the bought thing says, sorry, I couldn't give you anything of me, so here's this instead. Second, what a portion of yourself looks like. Emerson gives a list.
The poet brings a poem, the shepherd a lamb, the farmer his corn, the painter his picture, and a girl a handkerchief she sewed herself. Each gives what passed through their own hands and life.
The value isn't the price; it's that some of the giver is in it. Third, he isn't a scold.
In the same essay he calls flowers and fruits fit presents, and admits that giving and receiving are awkward, tangled things. The point isn't never to buy anything.
It's to notice the difference between a present that carries you and one that only stands in for you.

teach.h: THE WEEK'S THREAD: THE REAL THING.

teach.b: This week Emerson asked us to hold self and others together, to watch what comes back, to feel contained in something larger, to draw another circle, to act with enthusiasm, to be sincere with a friend.
Read side by side, they make the same request in different rooms: the real thing, not a stand-in. A sincere word instead of a polished one. A whole effort instead of a half one.

teach.h: THE ONLY GIFT IS A PORTION OF THYSELF.
teach.b: A portion of yourself instead of an apology for one.

how: Readers who take Emerson's Gifts to heart often give handmade or personal things, a letter, a meal, something they grew or wrote, alongside or instead of bought presents.

o: the belief that only costly presents show true love
a rule that every gift must be returned with a gift
Emerson's claim that a real gift carries some of the giver

games.q: inside Emerson's Gifts: tap the pairs.

s: Emerson says you should never buy anyone a present
he calls flowers and fruits fit presents. his point is the difference between a gift that carries you and one that stands in for you.
Emerson calls rings and jewels apologies for gifts
"rings and other jewels are not gifts, but apologies for gifts."
in Emerson's list, the painter brings money
the painter brings his picture: something that passed through his own hands.

games.q: you're a farmer in Emerson's list, and a friend's birthday is coming. what do you bring?
games.why: Emerson: the farmer brings corn, the shepherd his lamb, the poet his poem. "the only gift is a portion of thyself."

practice: Let one person come to mind who could use a small kindness this week, and ask what you could make for them, not buy: a note in your own handwriting, a meal, a photo you took, a repair.
Picture handing it over, and notice what of you is in it.

carryVoice: Your line: a portion of myself. The price was never the point. Rest well.
